drills.q: Compute success probability of a depth-800 circuit at two-qubit error 1e-3.
drills.a: exp(-800 * 1e-3) = exp(-0.8) ~ 0.45. Rule of thumb: every ~1000 two-qubit gates at p2=1e-3 costs e-fold (~37% survival).

drills.q: 3-qubit repetition code: what does the syndrome (s01=True, s12=False) tell you?
drills.a: Qubits 0 and 1 disagree, qubits 1 and 2 agree -> qubit 0 flipped. Apply X on qubit 0. Syndrome pairs localize a single X error exactly.

drills.q: Why can't the naive 'is state still in code space' check detect triple errors in the repetition code?
drills.a: XXX maps |000> to |111> and |111> to |000>: a permutation of codewords. The state stays in code space while carrying wrong amplitudes; only amplitude overlap against the original detects it.

drills.q: Estimate physical qubits for one logical qubit at target logical error 1e-9 with p=1e-3 (surface code).
drills.a: Need 0.1^((d+1)/2) <= 1e-8 -> (d+1)/2 >= 8 -> d >= 15 (use 17 for margin). Qubits ~ 2d^2: d=17 -> 578 physical/logical.

drills.q: Two vendors claim logical qubits: A says 50 @ 2:1 encoding, B says 200 logical planned on ~10k+ physical. Which question separates them?
drills.a: What logical operations run fault-tolerantly and at what magic-state/routing cost? Memory-level encoding (A) is cheap; algorithm-capable logical machines need gate sets + factories + routing (B). Demand Lambda and decoder latency too.

drills.q: Your decoder p99 latency exceeds the 1us stabiliser round under load. Consequences and mitigations?
drills.a: Backlog stalls rounds or forces drops - both convert directly into logical error since idle/lost cycles accumulate memory errors. Mitigate: bounded-latency decoders (union-find), FPGA offload, admission control that pauses rounds before overflow.

drills.q: Explain why halving physical error p saves roughly 4x qubits at fixed target logical error.
drills.a: eps_L ~ (100p)^((d+1)/2): halving p moves you one full exponent step down per distance unit... concretely log(eps)/log(100p) shrinks by ~1, so required (d+1)/2 drops by ~1, i.e., d by 2, and cost 2d^2 falls by factor ~(d/(d-2))^2 ~ 4x near d~25.

drills.q: Why do trapped-ion platforms favour different codes than superconducting?
drills.a: Ions have all-to-all connectivity and slow gates (~300us) vs superconducting nearest-neighbour fast (~50ns). High-rate small-block codes exploiting connectivity suit ions; planar surface codes suit superconducting layout constraints despite overhead.

drills.q: Connect QEC progress to PQC migration urgency in two sentences.
drills.a: RSA-2048 estimates (20M qubits / 8h) are QEC-overhead arithmetic: below-threshold operation plus ~1000:1 encoding plus magic factories. Each fidelity or code improvement compresses that multiplier, so migration deadlines hedge against QEC engineering accelerating, not just hardware scaling.

drills.q: Willow showed logical lifetime beating best physical qubit ~5x. Why did that matter commercially?
drills.a: It converts threshold theory into demonstrated engineering: memory persists longer encoded than raw, meaning added qubits now buy reliability instead of noise. Every roadmap qubit-count estimate assumes exactly this regime; it was the first direct superconducting proof.

drills.q: A team wants to plan a 5-year roadmap assuming fault-tolerant computers capable of breaking RSA-2048 will exist by year 3, citing 2026's below-threshold demonstration. Evaluate this assumption.
drills.a: The premise is accurate but the inference isn't supported â€” 2026's demonstrations involve small logical qubit counts (12) for short computations, while RSA-2048 needs an estimated hundreds of thousands to ~1M physical qubits sustained through a deep circuit, several more orders of magnitude beyond what's shown. Treat 'year 3' as one scenario among a wide expert range (roughly 5-30 years), not a committed timeline.

drills.q: Given hardware timeline uncertainty, should post-quantum cryptography migration planning wait for more clarity?
drills.a: No â€” migration timelines are driven by data sensitivity duration and how long real migrations take (often years), not by pinning the exact year a quantum computer arrives. The harvest-now-decrypt-later threat model means data encrypted today with vulnerable algorithms is already at risk regardless of when decryption capability arrives.
